# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-39 (Extended v246)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to autumn Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Charlemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven, Quenford. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring/summer Year 10 English subplot; autumn Year 10 current time.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 39, autumn Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt (spring Year 10). Harine swore to wife of Sebin Brackick to teach children of Kelmere their letters (summer Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed her within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.

**Summer Year 10 births and changes**: Ismira Stenson died from festering wound; buried at Kelmere; bone compass went to Matho Stenson. Son born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick, named Brevus Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe. Daughter born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick, named Elvie Brackick; family lived in Torton. Son born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge, named Madan Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere. Febin Prydenridge packed single trunk and moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven. Davus was apprenticed anew and became a mason. Daughter born to Movie Prydenridge and Thizek Stenenridge, named Kamira Stenenridge; family lived in Elmhaven.

**Chapter 38-39 summer/autumn scenes and movements**: Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage; wind carried salt and tar smell; carts loaded with turnips creaked past well; smoke lay flat over fields; frost silvered hedges overnight; rain threatened but held off; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; baker's boy was late, line at oven grew long. Multiple characters counted coins twice and came up penny short; complained of aching back; read almanac aloud mispronouncing saints; laughed at stories nobody else found funny; mended torn sleeves by window; fell asleep in chairs before fire caught; walked long way round to avoid muddy square. **Ilrald Prydenridge left Torton and settled in Wilwick. Dalis left Torton and settled in Yarlby. Harine went along to live in Wilwick as well. Jotho Thornmere quit Ostcombe for good and took lodgings in Quenford. Yera Stenworth followed him to Quenford within the month.** RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. RUMOR—In letter Semor Brackick burned, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Luvie bought a ribbon at stall and regretted it. "Price of salt is a scandal," said Luena Stenenridge and Jotho echoed it. River is up again in spring, remarked Luvie Prydenridge and Nerine Prydenridge agreed it always was. Jotho Thornmere argued with carter over price of oats; told Lura Haskick she looked tired (did not deny); Yera Stenworth hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step; Lura complained of aching back; Peten Haskick asked if rain coming, Jotho only shrugged; children chased hoop down lane shrieking.

**New death**: Marald Corrford died from fall from mill loft at Ravenmere; laid in churchyard at Ravenmere.

**New event**: Parcel from Lura Haskick reached Bremira Corrford containing silver chalice; now Bremira's to keep.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Imprisonment, Escape Plan, Faria's Illness and Treasure Revelation

**Edmond Dantès' arrest and Villefort's conspiracy (1 March 1814)**: Young sailor jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent. Magistrate arrested Dantès during feast. Villefort interrogated Dantès about commission to deliver letter in Paris to Noirtier (Villefort's father). **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.** Mercédès came to Villefort's door inquiring; Villefort closed door. **Dantès was doomed.** Villefort reported conspiracy to King Louis XVIII, received Legion of Honor cross. **Noirtier—Villefort's father—disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, walked past sentries with bamboo switch.**

**Dantès' psychological dissolution (1 March 1814–Year 4+)**: Boarded boat to Frioul; saw Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt; reached Château d'If. Locked in bare underground chamber. Marked plaster fragment daily with 30 July 1816 reckoning. Expected release in fortnight; waited nearly four years. Governor transferred; Edmond became number 34. At end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride, then doubt, then supplication. Asked for companion; refused. Gloom, rage, blasphemies ensued. Contemplation of abyss offered strange consolation. **Resolved: "I wish to die." Chose starvation; swore oath. Heard mysterious scratching—subterranean workman mining way. "If neighbor would not come, he would go to neighbor." Worked tirelessly extracting plaster and stone. Noted prisoner on other side ceased labor. After hours, iron met smooth surface—beam blocking hole. Must dig above or under it.**

**Abbé Faria revealed and initial connection (Chapter 38)**: **Dantès made passionate plea: "Oh, I am a Christian... I conjure you do not abandon me... I shall love you as I loved my father."** **Following night Dantès rose, dispersed fragments, pushed bed back, gave himself to happiness.** **Next morning appeared head, then shoulders: small stature man, hair blanched by suffering rather than age. Deep-set penetrating eye beneath thick gray eyebrow, long black beard to breast. Thin deeply furrowed face; numbered sixty or sixty-five years. Stranger identified as: "I am Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811; previously confined three years in Fenestrelle fortress. In 1811 transferred to Piedmont. Learned Napoleon had son named king of Rome."** **Faria imprisoned because in 1807 he dreamed plan Napoleon realized in 1811; sought one large compact powerful empire instead of petty Italian principalities. Plan will never succeed; Italy fated to misfortune. "I am poor mad prisoner of Château d'If, permitted many years to amuse visitors with my insanity."**

**Faria's scholarly achievements and education of Dantès (Chapters 38-39)**: **Possessed five thousand volumes in Rome library; found one hundred fifty well-chosen books possess all man needs. Recites Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes, Dante, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Machiavelli, Bossuet. Made vocabulary of necessary words; knows one thousand. Made excellent pens from whiting-head cartilages. Wrote _A Treatise on Possibility of General Monarchy in Italy_—sixty-eight weeks. Tore up two shirts and handkerchiefs to complete pages. Wrote with own blood for important notes. Dissolved soot in Sunday wine for ink.** **Proposed escape: "We must pierce corridor by forming side opening about middle like cross top... kill sentinel who guards it, make escape."** **Why did not kill sentinel: "Natural repugnance to crime prevented thinking of it... man loathes idea of blood."** **Carefully preserved rope ladder of cords twenty-five to thirty feet, concealed behind fitting stone at bed's head.** **Dantès requested education; Faria responded: "When I have taught you mathematics, physics, history, and three or four modern languages, you will know as much as I do myself. It will scarcely require two years for me to communicate the stock of learning I possess."** **Dantès possessed prodigious memory, astonishing quickness of conception, mathematical turn of mind. Already knew Italian and little Romaic dialect from East voyages; by aid of these two languages easily comprehended construction of all others. At end of six months began to speak Spanish, English, and German.**

**Escape tunnel construction (over fifteen months, Chapter 39)**: **Faria showed sketch: plan of his cell and Dantès' cell with passage uniting them. In passage proposed to drive a level; would bring two prisoners beneath gallery where sentry kept watch. Large excavation would be made, and one flagstone would be completely loosened, giving way beneath soldier's feet. Stunned sentry immediately bound and gagged by Dantès. Make way through gallery window, let themselves down by abbé's rope ladder.** **Miners began labors with vigor. Nothing interrupted progress except necessity of returning before turnkey's visits. Learned to distinguish almost imperceptible sound of jailer's footsteps. Fresh earth excavated thrown out of window; rubbish pulverized so finely night wind carried it far away.** **More than a year consumed with only tools: chisel, knife, wooden lever. Faria continued instruction in languages and history. At end of fifteen months level finished, excavation completed beneath gallery. Two workmen distinctly heard measured tread of sentinel pacing overhead. Compelled to await sufficiently dark night to favor flight, propped flagstone with small beam from walls. Greatest dread lest stone give way before right time.**

**Faria's cataleptic attack (Chapter 39)**: **Faria seized with terrible, perhaps mortal illness; had similar attack year before imprisonment. Instructed Dantès: go to his cell, draw out one of bed's feet, find small phial half-filled with red-looking fluid. Help him back to room while he had strength.** **Warned: "When catalepsy comes to its height I shall lie still and motionless as though dead, uttering neither sigh nor groan. Symptoms may be much more violent, fearful convulsions, foam at mouth, cry out loudly. Take care my cries are not heard, for if they are I should be removed to another part of prison, and we be separated forever. When I become quite motionless, cold, rigid as corpse, then force open my teeth with knife, pour from eight to ten drops of liquor down my throat, and I may perhaps revive."** **Fit lasted two hours; Dantès prevented cries by covering head with blanket. Old man more helpless than infant, colder and paler than marble, crushed and broken as reed trampled. Edmond waited till life seemed extinct, then took knife, forced open jaws, administered appointed number of drops, anxiously awaited result.** **Hour passed; old man gave no sign. Dantès feared he had delayed too long. At length slight color tinged livid cheeks, consciousness returned to dull eyeballs, faint sigh issued from lips, sufferer made feeble effort to move.** **Dantès sprinted to entrance, drew stone over opening, hurried to his cell. Jailer saw prisoner seated on bed. Before jailer's departing steps died away, Dantès hurried back to abbé's chamber, raised stone, found Faria beside him, fully regained consciousness but helpless and exhausted.** **Faria reported: "Last attack lasted half hour, after it I was hungry, got up without help. Now I can move neither right arm nor leg, and my head seems uncomfortable, showing suffusion of blood on brain. Third attack will either carry me off, or leave me paralyzed for life."** **Dantès insisted: "You will not die! Your third attack will find you at liberty. We shall save you another time, with better chance of success."** **Faria revealed: "Since first attack of this malady, I have continually reflected on it. I expected it, for it is a family inheritance; both my father and grandfather died of it in a third attack. Physician who prepared remedy I have twice successfully taken was celebrated Cabanis, and he predicted similar end for me."** **Dantès, as sailor and swimmer, knew man so loaded would sink before fifty strokes. Faria said: "Here I shall remain till hour of my deliverance arrives, and that in all human probability will be hour of my death. As for you, who are young and active, delay not on my account, but fly. I give you back your promise."** **Instructed Dantès: "Fill up excavation beneath soldier's gallery; he might hear hollow sound of his footsteps and call attention of his officer to circumstance. That would bring discovery leading to separation. Set about this work, keep at it all night if necessary. Do not return here tomorrow till after jailer has visited me. I shall have something of greatest importance to communicate to you."**

**Faria's treasure revelation (Chapter 39)**: **When Dantès returned next morning, found Faria seated and looking composed. In ray of light from narrow window, he held open in left hand (of which alone he retained use) a sheet of paper, constantly rolled into small compass, having form of cylinder, not easily kept open.** **Faria revealed he was secretary and intimate friend of Cardinal Spada, last of the princes of that name; owed his all happiness to this worthy lord. Cardinal not rich although wealth of family had passed into proverb. Faria was tutor to cardinal's nephews, now dead; when cardinal alone in world, Faria devoted himself to his will. Cardinal's house had no secrets for Faria. Often saw patron annotating ancient volumes and searching manuscripts.** **One day when Faria reproached cardinal for unavailing searches and lamented his resulting despair, cardinal smiled bitterly, opened volume relating to History of City of Rome. In twentieth chapter of Life of Pope Alexander VI. were lines Faria never forgot:** **Pope and Cæsar Borgia needed money after wars of Romagna ended; determined to make two cardinals from greatest personages of Rome, especially rich men. Plan: sell great appointments and splendid offices the cardinals held; then sell the two cardinal hats besides. Selected Giovanni Rospigliosi (held four highest dignities of Holy See) and Cæsar Spada (noblest and richest Roman nobility); both felt high honor of favor. Rospigliosi and Spada paid for being cardinals; eight other persons paid for offices cardinals held before elevation; thus eight hundred thousand crowns entered coffers of speculators.** **Then pope heaped attentions upon Rospigliosi and Spada, conferred cardinal insignia, induced them to arrange affairs and take up residence at Rome. Pope and Cæsar Borgia invited two cardinals to dinner—matter of dispute between Holy Father and son. Cæsar thought to use one of his means: famous key given to certain persons with request to open designated cupboard, furnished with small iron point negligently made. When pressed to effect opening, person pricked by point and died next day. Also ring with lion's head that Cæsar wore when greeting friends with clasp of hand; lion bit hand thus favored, bite mortal at end of twenty-four hours.** **Dantès happy to escape history that would confirm belief in friend's mental instability, glided like snake along narrow passage; Faria, restored by alarm to certain activity, pushed stone into place with foot and covered with mat to avoid discovery. Faria sat to receive governor, avoiding gestures to conceal paralysis that had half stricken him with death. Fear lest governor, touched with pity, order removal to better quarters, thus separate him from young companion. Fortunately governor left convinced poor madman only troubled with slight indisposition.**

## Marius and Cosette: Marriage and Jean Valjean's Death

**Wedding and immediate aftermath (1 February 1833)**: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration. Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.** **Jean Valjean proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. Complete extinction ensued.

**Jean Valjean's decline and death**: Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented substitution method; six hundred thousand francs made.** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** **Lies in Père-Lachaise cemetery vicinity common grave, far from elegant quarter, deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus.**

**Thénardier's blackmail and confrontation**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right; claimed twenty thousand francs as price. Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With monkey agility, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.** **Marius revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15 June 1832: Javert owed life to insurgent who fired into air instead of blowing out brains. Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. Condemned Thénardier as "infamous wretch," "liar," "calumniator," "villain." Noted witnessed Thénardier Jondrette in lair on Rue de l'Hôpital; succeeded only in glorifying Jean Valjean.** **Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered Thénardier to America with daughter; wife dead. Thénardier set up as slave-dealer in America, morally irremediable.**
